paragraphs.heading: Wandering in the dark
paragraphs.edited: Several years ago, I was in a brand new apartment. I woke up in the middle of the night to do something — I don't remember what it was. As I went back to bed, I rammed my toe so hard into the bed frame that I ended up breaking my toe. I didn't know I had broken it until I woke up the next morning. It was black and blue, my whole foot was all messed up, and I limped around for days. The doctor told me there was nothing that could be done about it, because I had simply broken my toe. The bed wasn't new, but the apartment was. When I woke up, it was pitch black and I couldn't see a thing. Naturally, I was so disoriented — I didn't know where I was, I didn't know what was going on — that I forgot where the bed was, because I forgot where I was.

paragraphs.edited: Growing up, in my younger days as an early baby Christian, that's about how I thought of faith. I thought of faith as wandering in the darkness, trying to figure something out, hoping I don't stub my toe and hoping I don't do something dumb. And in reality, in my life, I actually did stub my toe, to the point where I walked away for quite some time. As I came back to the church, I realized something: faith is not at all like wandering in the darkness. What I've discovered is that so many students still hold that belief — that faith is either attaching themselves to what their parents believe and simply going along with something, or literally wandering around in the darkness, hoping that what they believe is somehow true, and that somehow at the end of all things, when this life ends, they'll find out that it actually is true.

paragraphs.heading: What John says about faith
paragraphs.edited: What's interesting, though, is that John says something at the very end of his gospel that starts to speak to us about what faith actually is. It's in John chapter 20, verses 30 and 31, and John says this: "Jesus did many other miracles, or miraculous signs, in the presence of his disciples, which are not recorded in this book, but these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name."
paragraphs.exact: What's interesting though, is that John says something in the very end of his gospel that starts to speak to us about really what faith actually is. And it's in John chapter 20 verses 30 and 31. And John says this, Jesus did many other miracles or miraculous signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not recorded in this book. But these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.

paragraphs.edited: What's interesting is what John says here: that these miraculous signs, all of these things John has recorded in his gospel, are there so that you might believe — we are given reasons. And what's fascinating about the gospel of John is the seven miraculous signs that John gives, starting with Jesus turning water into wine and then ending with that magnitude of a miracle, the raising of Lazarus. And then, if you want to include the eighth one, Jesus' own resurrection — time after time, John sets it up so that we see, increasing in measure, all these signs that Jesus is exactly who he says he is. This is what we want students to actually get: that biblical faith is trust based on evidence, and that translates into a deeper relationship.

paragraphs.heading: Trust grows a relationship
paragraphs.edited: Think about the relationships that you have. You don't just blindly trust somebody you don't know, but the more you get to know somebody, the more you trust them. The more you trust them, the deeper that relationship starts to go. That's how relationships work, and it's no different with our relationship with Christ. The more we know who he is, the more we know about what's going on and what the gospel is, the more we can trust — and the more reason we have to trust in what God is doing through Christ. And the more that we do that, the deeper our relationship with him goes.

paragraphs.heading: Hebrews 11 and certainty
paragraphs.edited: What's even more fascinating, I think, is that when we start thinking about what faith is and how this works, we naturally find ourselves in Hebrews 11. Hebrews 11:1: "Now faith is being sure of what we hope for and certain of what we do not see. This is what the ancients were commended for." Then the writer of Hebrews goes through that huge wall of faith, all these people who had the right kind of faith. We use this verse as the foundational piece of what faith means: being sure of what we hope for and certain of what we do not see. Well, that word "certain" — the word actually means, or has with it, the idea of a foundation or a substructure.

paragraphs.edited: So think of it this way: it's a basement. The idea the writer is talking about is the basement in your home. When you walk downstairs into your basement — if you have one, or if you've ever walked into a basement — you generally don't fear that the whole house is going to cave in on you. Because when you've walked down into a basement, it has these huge metal beams and these metal poles, and they're driven into the cement, into the ground, and the whole house is being held up by those beams and that basement. And when you walk downstairs, you don't think anything of it. Why? Because the house is built on a solid foundation. If the foundation in the house is cracked, the house is starting to be no good, and you can't really do anything in the house until you fix the foundation.
